analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for the government to block corporate mergers that reduce competition, raise prices, or push down wages.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Senator Klobuchar with three Democratic cosponsors in November 2021, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the nation's merger laws to make it harder for large companies to buy their way to dominance. Under current law, the government must prove a merger would 'substantially lessen competition' — a high bar that courts have made even higher. The bill would lower that bar to an 'appreciable risk of materially lessening competition,' make it illegal to merge toward a monopsony (a single dominant buyer of labor or supplies, which can push wages down), and force the largest merging companies — deals over $5 billion, or involving firms worth over $100 billion — to prove their own merger is harmless rather than making the government prove it isn't. It would also create a new FTC office to track industry concentration, study whether big deals actually delivered the promised benefits, and require annual reporting from companies that settle merger cases.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, who would face fewer deals that lead to higher prices and less choice; workers, who would gain new protection against employers consolidating until they can hold wages down; small businesses and startups, which would face less risk of being bought or squeezed by dominant firms; and antitrust enforcers, who would get clearer rules, more data, and an easier path to winning merger cases.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the 'substantially lessens competition' standard with an 'appreciable risk of materially lessening competition' standard, making it easier to stop harmful mergers early.
Adds monopsony power to the Clayton Act, so mergers that concentrate buyer power over workers or suppliers — the mechanism behind depressed wages — can be blocked.

Shifts the burden of proof to the merging companies for very large deals (over $5 billion) or deals involving firms over $100 billion in market value, so the biggest companies must prove a merger is safe rather than the government proving it is harmful.

Creates an Office of the Competition Advocate at the FTC to track market concentration, publish data, and investigate whether consummated mergers harmed prices, wages, quality, or innovation — including whether companies delivered the benefits they promised to win approval.
Requires companies that settle merger cases to report for five years on pricing, quality, and whether claimed efficiencies were actually passed to consumers.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations and their investors, especially those in concentrated industries and frequent acquirers, which would face a higher bar to close mergers and more scrutiny of deals already made; mergers-and-acquisitions advisors — investment banks, law firms, and consultants — who would see fewer and slower deals; and very large companies in general, which would face new reporting and investigation requirements.

drawbacks.text: The lower legal standard and presumption of harm for very large deals could also stop or delay mergers that genuinely create efficiencies, lower costs, or rescue struggling companies, raising the cost of deals for everyone.

Requiring parties to prove a merger's harmlessness ('establish by a preponderance of the evidence' the deal is safe) would lengthen and raise the cost of merger review, a burden critics of similar proposals argued falls hardest on smaller acquirers trying to compete with incumbents.

The bill's centerpiece is enforcement and data collection; it depends heavily on the priorities of future administrations and FTC leadership to actually block mergers, and it does not directly lower any specific price or raise any specific wage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits would be broad and slow: fewer mergers that concentrate market power, with knock-on effects for prices, wages, and small business formation. Its costs would be real but narrower: more expensive merger reviews and a risk of blocking some deals that would have been pro-competitive. The honest weighing is that the bill changed the defaults in favor of enforcers rather than corporations, and whether the trade is worth it depends on how much one believes today's courts under-enforce — a belief the bill's findings section documents in detail but which remains a judgment call.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in November 2021 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, it sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar introduced the bill on November 18, 2021, joined by Senators Blumenthal, Hirono, and Booker as cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced — the only substantive action it ever received.
The committee took no further action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded for the remainder of the 117th Congress, which ended January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that rely on acquisitions — large platforms and consolidating industries — and the investment banks and law firms that advise on mergers were better off because the bill never advanced; merger law stayed exactly as it was.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that buy competitors, and merger advisors

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor; it was her signature merger-law reform proposal.

for.name: Sens. Richard Blumenthal, Mazie Hirono, and Cory Booker

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats, no Republican cosponsored, and because the bill never got a hearing or vote, no one else's position was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Large corporations in concentrated markets (including big tech platforms)
industries.note: The bill presumes harm for deals over $5 billion and for firms over $100 billion in market value, and shifts the burden of proof onto them. Their continued ability to buy competitors is a main reason prices stay high and wages stay low in concentrated markets, so their interest in killing the bill ran against consumers and workers.

industries.industry: Mergers-and-acquisitions industry (investment banks, deal lawyers, consultants)
industries.note: Stricter standards, burden-shifting, mandatory post-settlement reporting, and post-merger investigations all mean fewer, slower, costlier deals. Deal volume is these firms' revenue.

industries.industry: Small businesses, startups, and new entrants
industries.note: The bill cites reduced new business formation as a core harm of concentration, and a lower bar against acquisitions of nascent rivals makes it easier for new firms to grow without being bought. Its findings tie competition to small business growth and lower economic inequality.
